Council at Virata's Court After the Exil: The diplomacy before the Kurukshetra war is narrated in the Udyoga Parva ('Book of Effort/Preparation'), the fifth of the eighteen parvas of the Mahabharata.

After the thirteenth year ended, the Pandavas revealed themselves at the court of King Virata of Matsya, and Abhimanyu married Virata's daughter Uttara; the Pandavas then based themselves at Upaplavya, a town in Virata's kingdom.
Exile terms set at the second dice game: Forest exile 12 years | Incognito year 1 | Total 13 years.

Duryodhana claimed Arjuna had been recognised before the thirteenth year was complete; in the Virata Parva Bhishma reckoned, counting intercalary months, that the term had been fulfilled with about five months and twelve nights to spare.
Bhishma's reckoning of the surplus beyond 13 years: Months 5 | Nights 12.
At the council in Virata's assembly hall, Krishna proposed sending a worthy envoy to ask Duryodhana to return half the kingdom to Yudhishthira.
Balarama urged conciliation and partly blamed Yudhishthira for gambling knowingly against the skilled Shakuni; Satyaki angrily rejected this view.
Drupada advised preparing for war while negotiating: sending messengers to allied kings to request troops and sending his own priest as envoy to Hastinapura.
Drupada's Envoy to Hastinapura: Drupada's envoy was his family priest (purohita), who is not named in the text; he went to Hastinapura on the Pandavas' behalf.
Drupada's priest reminded the Kuru court of the Pandavas' wrongs (the lac house, the dice game, the exile) and asked for the return of their share of the kingdom.
Bhishma received Drupada's envoy favourably and acknowledged the justice of the Pandavas' claim while warning against war with Arjuna.
Karna interrupted Bhishma in the assembly, insisting that the Pandavas had broken the exile terms and should return to the forest; Bhishma rebuked him.
Dhritarashtra calmed the assembly and replied that he would send his own minister and charioteer Sanjaya to the Pandavas after deliberation.
Seeking Allies — Arjuna and Duryodhana a: Arjuna and Duryodhana both travelled to Dvaraka to seek Krishna's help and arrived on the same day while Krishna was asleep.
Duryodhana entered first and sat on a fine seat at the head of Krishna's bed; Arjuna, arriving after him, stood at the foot of the bed with folded hands.
On waking, Krishna saw Arjuna first; since Duryodhana had arrived first but Arjuna was seen first (and was the younger), Krishna offered Arjuna the first choice.
Krishna offered two alternatives: himself alone, unarmed and not fighting in the battle, or a huge force of cowherd warriors called the Narayanas (the Narayani army).

The Narayani army is described in the Udyoga Parva as an arbuda of gopa warriors equal to Krishna in strength; arbuda is a very large number, rendered by translators as ten million or a hundred million, so no exact size is reliable.
Arjuna chose Krishna alone; Duryodhana, delighted, took the Narayani army, which fought on the Kaurava side.
Arjuna then asked Krishna to be his charioteer, and Krishna agreed.
Balarama told Duryodhana he would fight for neither side, since he could not oppose Krishna; he later left on a pilgrimage along the Sarasvati river during the war.
Kritavarma, a Yadava chief of the Bhoja/Andhaka clans, gave Duryodhana an akshauhini of his own troops, separate from the Narayani army.
Satyaki (Yuyudhana), a Vrishni warrior and Arjuna's pupil, joined the Pandavas with an akshauhini — so Yadava forces fought on both sides.
Shalya Tricked onto the Kaurava Side: Shalya, king of Madra and brother of Madri (thus maternal uncle of Nakula and Sahadeva), set out with a large army (an akshauhini) intending to join the Pandavas.
Duryodhana had pavilions and lavish refreshments prepared along Shalya's route; Shalya, believing Yudhishthira had arranged them, offered a boon to whoever was his host.
Duryodhana revealed himself and asked Shalya to lead/fight with his army; bound by his word, Shalya agreed to fight for the Kauravas.

Shalya then visited Yudhishthira and explained what had happened; Yudhishthira asked him, if he were ever made Karna's charioteer in the duel with Arjuna, to sap Karna's confidence (tejovadha), and Shalya agreed.
During this visit Shalya consoled Yudhishthira with the tale of Indra's victory over Vritra and the fall of Nahusha (the Indravijaya episode), a story of suffering followed by restoration.
Shalya kept his promise on day 17, when as Karna's charioteer he repeatedly belittled Karna, including the parable of the crow and the swans.
Sanjaya's Embassy to the Pandavas: Sanjaya's embassy is told in the Sanjayayana sub-parva of the Udyoga Parva; Dhritarashtra sent his charioteer Sanjaya to the Pandavas at Upaplavya.

Sanjaya conveyed Dhritarashtra's wish for peace but offered no restoration of the kingdom; he argued that war against kinsmen was sinful and that even living on alms would be better than winning by slaughter.
Yudhishthira replied that he wanted peace and would accept it if Indraprastha (his share of the kingdom) were returned, but that his claim rested on dharma.
Krishna answered Sanjaya forcefully, arguing that action in accord with one's duty is necessary and that a kshatriya's recovery of a stolen kingdom is righteous.
Yudhishthira sent word through Sanjaya that he would settle for just five villages — one for each brother — if that would avert war.
Arjuna sent Duryodhana a stern warning through Sanjaya about the destruction the Pandavas, Krishna and the Gandiva bow would cause.
Sanjaya returned at night and delivered the Pandavas' replies the next morning in the Kuru assembly; Dhritarashtra wavered but Duryodhana refused any concession.
The Five Villages — Names by Version: The five-villages offer is made by Yudhishthira in the Udyoga Parva through Sanjaya, and Yudhishthira repeats it to Krishna before Krishna's peace mission.

In the Sanskrit text four villages are named and the fifth is left open; the Critical Edition reads Avisthala, Vrikasthala, Makandi and Varanavata, while other editions and translations (e.g. K. M. Ganguli's) read Kushasthala for Avisthala and, in one of the two passages, Asandi for Makandi.
Text-based list of the five villages (readings vary): Avisthala or Kushasthala | Vrikasthala | Makandi or Asandi | Varanavata | any fifth village of Duryodhana's choosing.

A popular north Indian tradition instead names five 'prasthas' — Indraprastha, Swarnaprastha, Panaprastha, Vyaghraprastha and Tilaprastha, traditionally identified with Delhi, Sonipat, Panipat, Baghpat and Tilpat — which is a folk tradition, not the epic's list.
Many popular retellings and screen adaptations move the five-villages demand into Krishna's speech at the Kuru court; in the Sanskrit epic it originates in Yudhishthira's message via Sanjaya.
Duryodhana's famous refusal — that he would not yield even as much land as the point of a sharp needle can pierce — is spoken in the Kuru assembly during Krishna's peace mission (Udyoga Parva).
The Sleepless Night — Vidura Niti and Sa: After Sanjaya's report, Dhritarashtra could not sleep and summoned Vidura; this section of the Udyoga Parva is called Prajagara ('Vigil').

Vidura's counsel to the sleepless king, known as Vidura Niti, is a collection of maxims on statecraft, prudence, the qualities of wise and foolish men, and the dangers of greed; it is often excerpted as an independent text.
Vidura urged Dhritarashtra to restore the Pandavas' share and restrain Duryodhana, warning that the Kuru house would otherwise be destroyed.
Vidura then called the ancient sage Sanatsujata, whose teaching to Dhritarashtra on death, immortality, self-knowledge and Brahman forms the Sanatsujatiya (Sanatsujata Parva).
Shankara is traditionally credited with a commentary on the Sanatsujatiya, showing its importance as a philosophical text alongside the Bhagavad Gita.
Krishna's Peace Mission — Preparations: Krishna's journey as envoy to Hastinapura is the Bhagavadyana sub-parva ('The Lord's Journey') of the Udyoga Parva.
Before Krishna left Upaplavya, each Pandava gave his view: Yudhishthira wanted peace even at a cost; Bhima unexpectedly spoke for peace, and Krishna goaded him by questioning his courage.
Arjuna told Krishna to do what he thought best; Nakula favoured peace; Sahadeva and Satyaki argued for war.
Draupadi held up her long, unbound hair — dishevelled since the dice-game humiliation — and demanded that Krishna remember it if the Kauravas sought peace without justice.
The Udyoga Parva says Krishna set out at the end of autumn, in the month called Kaumuda (usually identified with Kartika), under the Revati asterism.
Krishna travelled with Satyaki; on the way he met sages including Parashurama and others who wished to witness the assembly.
Krishna in the Kuru Court: In Hastinapura Krishna first called on Dhritarashtra, then lodged at Vidura's house and visited his aunt Kunti, who was living there.

Before Krishna left Hastinapura, Kunti gave him a message for Yudhishthira urging him to fight for his kingdom, framed by the old tale of Vidula, a queen who roused her defeated son to rise and fight (the Vidula episode, Udyoga Parva).
Krishna declined Duryodhana's invitation to dine, explaining that one eats another's food either out of affection or out of need, and neither applied; he ate at Vidura's house instead.
In the assembly Krishna appealed to Dhritarashtra to restrain his son and restore the Pandavas' share, warning that the Kuru line would perish otherwise.

Sages in the assembly supported Krishna with cautionary tales: Parashurama told of the proud king Dambhodbhava humbled by Nara and Narayana; Kanva told the story of Matali; Narada told the story of Galava.
Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and Dhritarashtra all urged Duryodhana to make peace; Duryodhana insisted he had done no wrong and would give nothing.
Gandhari was summoned to the assembly and rebuked her son, telling him that the kingdom could not be enjoyed by one who could not control himself; Duryodhana walked out.
Duryodhana's vow in the court: not even land as much as a needle's point would be yielded to the Pandavas without war.
Vishvarupa in the Court and the Plot to: Duryodhana, with Karna, Shakuni and Duhshasana, plotted to seize and imprison Krishna, the envoy, in the assembly.
Satyaki discovered the plot, posted troops at the gate and warned Krishna; Vidura denounced the scheme before Dhritarashtra.
Krishna laughed and revealed his universal form (vishvarupa) in the Kuru court: gods, sages and heroes — including the Pandavas and the Vrishnis — appeared emerging from his body, blazing with light.
Most kings shut their eyes before the vishvarupa in the court; according to the text Bhishma, Drona, Vidura, Sanjaya and the sages could behold it.
Dhritarashtra asked for and was granted divine sight for the moment so he could see Krishna's cosmic form, after which he asked to return to blindness, wishing to see nothing else.
The court vishvarupa (Udyoga Parva) is distinct from the more famous vishvarupa shown to Arjuna in Chapter 11 of the Bhagavad Gita on the battlefield.
After withdrawing the form, Krishna left the assembly; the peace mission had failed, and war became certain.
Krishna–Karna Meeting: The meeting is told in the Karnopanivada sub-parva ('Secret Talk with Karna'); as he left Hastinapura, Krishna took Karna alone in his chariot.
Krishna told Karna the secret of his birth: he was Kunti's first son, born before her marriage, and therefore by law (as a kanina son) a son of Pandu and the eldest Pandava.
Krishna offered Karna the throne: the Pandavas would serve him as their elder, Yudhishthira would be his heir apparent, and — in the text — Draupadi would come to him as well.

Karna refused: he owed his life and love to his foster parents Adhiratha and Radha, his wives and sons were of the suta community, and he could not betray Duryodhana, who had relied on him for thirteen years.
Karna asked Krishna to keep the secret from Yudhishthira, saying Yudhishthira would hand the kingdom to him if he knew, and he would only give it to Duryodhana.
Karna described the coming war as a great weapon-sacrifice with Krishna as its presiding priest, and recounted ominous dreams foretelling Kaurava defeat.
Krishna told Karna that the battle should begin on the new moon, about seven days later, and asked him to tell Bhishma, Drona and Kripa so.
Kunti–Karna Meeting: After Krishna's mission failed, Kunti went to Karna on the bank of the Ganga, where he was praying to the sun with his face to the east until midday.
Kunti revealed that she was his mother and that the Sun god Surya was his father, and begged him to join his brothers.
A voice from the sun (Surya) confirmed Kunti's words and urged Karna to obey his mother.
Karna reproached Kunti for abandoning him at birth and depriving him of his rank, and refused to change sides on the eve of war.
Karna promised Kunti he would not kill Yudhishthira, Bhima, Nakula or Sahadeva even when he could, but that he would fight Arjuna to the death.
Karna told Kunti she would always have five sons: either Arjuna or Karna would survive.
Karna kept the promise: at different points in the war he defeated and spared Yudhishthira, Bhima, Nakula and Sahadeva.

Kunti revealed Karna's birth to the Pandavas only after his death, at the water-offerings for the dead (Stri Parva); Yudhishthira grieves and, at the opening of the Shanti Parva in the Critical Edition (placed at the end of the Stri Parva in some editions), curses women never to be able to keep secrets.
Final Provocations — Uluka's Embassy and: When the armies were already assembled at Kurukshetra, Duryodhana sent Uluka, Shakuni's son, to the Pandavas with taunting, insulting messages (the Ulukadutagamana sub-parva).
Uluka's messages mocked the Pandavas' vows and Draupadi's humiliation; the Pandavas and Krishna replied with defiant counter-messages.
Rukmi, king of Bhojakata in Vidarbha and Rukmini's brother, came with an akshauhini offering help; Arjuna declined his boastful offer, and Duryodhana also declined, so Rukmi stayed out of the war.
Balarama and Rukmi are the two notable kings described as staying neutral in the war.

On the morning of the first day, Yudhishthira walked unarmed into the Kaurava ranks to seek the blessings of Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and Shalya; each blessed him and said that, bound to Duryodhana, he must fight for the Kauravas.
Yudhishthira then invited any warrior to cross over; Yuyutsu, Dhritarashtra's son by a vaishya woman, switched to the Pandava side before the battle began.
Udyoga Parva Structure and Recension Not: The Udyoga Parva's sub-parvas include: Sainyodyoga, Sanjayayana, Prajagara, Sanatsujata, Yanasandhi, Bhagavadyana, Karnopanivada, Abhiniryana, Bhishmabhishechana, Ulukadutagamana, Rathatirathasankhya and Ambopakhyana.
The Critical Edition (BORI, Pune) Udyoga Parva has 197 chapters; vulgate editions differ in chapter numbering.
Popular retellings often compress the embassies: Drupada's priest and Sanjaya are frequently omitted and Krishna alone is shown demanding five villages.
Some popular versions dramatise Duryodhana attempting to bind Krishna with ropes and the ropes failing; the Sanskrit text describes a plot discovered by Satyaki and the display of the universal form.
Numbers of the Narayani army and some envoy details vary between manuscripts and translations; the five village names differ between the Critical Edition and other editions.

The Akshauhini — Composition: The akshauhini, the unit in which the epic counts armies, is defined in the Adi Parva (Parvasangraha) by the narrator Ugrashravas.
One akshauhini: Chariots 21870 | Elephants 21870 | Cavalry (horses) 65610 | Infantry 109350 | Total units 218700.
Ratio within an akshauhini: Chariot 1 | Elephant 1 | Horse 3 | Foot soldier 5 — the same ratio as its smallest unit, the patti.

The text counts chariots, elephants, horses and foot soldiers but says nothing about charioteers, elephant riders, attendants or support personnel; modern commentators usually infer that these are not included, so real numbers would be larger (an inference, not a statement of the epic).

A frequently noted curiosity (a modern observation, not stated in the text): the digits of each akshauhini figure — 21870, 65610, 109350, 218700 — each add up to 18, echoing the 18 akshauhinis, 18 days and 18 parvas.
Historians treat the akshauhini totals as idealised or literary numbers rather than verified historical troop counts.
Akshauhini Unit Hierarchy: The smallest unit, the patti, consists of 1 chariot, 1 elephant, 3 horsemen and 5 foot soldiers.
Each higher unit is three times the previous, except the akshauhini, which is ten anikinis: patti, senamukha, gulma, gana, vahini, pritana, chamu, anikini, akshauhini.
Unit multipliers: Senamukha 3 pattis | Gulma 3 senamukhas | Gana 3 gulmas | Vahini 3 ganas | Pritana 3 vahinis | Chamu 3 pritanas | Anikini 3 chamus | Akshauhini 10 anikinis.
Chariots per unit level: Patti 1 | Senamukha 3 | Gulma 9 | Gana 27 | Vahini 81 | Pritana 243 | Chamu 729 | Anikini 2187 | Akshauhini 21870.
Total soldiers per unit level (1+1+3+5 = 10 per patti): Patti 10 | Senamukha 30 | Gulma 90 | Gana 270 | Vahini 810 | Pritana 2430 | Chamu 7290 | Anikini 21870 | Akshauhini 218700.
Total Forces at Kurukshetra: Eighteen akshauhinis assembled at Kurukshetra: seven for the Pandavas and eleven for the Kauravas.
Akshauhinis by side: Pandava 7 | Kaurava 11 | Total 18.
Total units by side (arithmetic from the akshauhini definition): Pandava 1530900 | Kaurava 2405700 | Both sides 3936600.
Pandava army (7 akshauhinis, computed): Chariots 153090 | Elephants 153090 | Cavalry 459270 | Infantry 765450.
Kaurava army (11 akshauhinis, computed): Chariots 240570 | Elephants 240570 | Cavalry 721710 | Infantry 1202850.
Both armies combined (18 akshauhinis, computed): Chariots 393660 | Elephants 393660 | Cavalry 1180980 | Infantry 1968300.
Share of total akshauhinis (percent, rounded): Pandava 38.9 | Kaurava 61.1.
The per-side totals above are calculated from the stated akshauhini definition; the epic itself gives the akshauhini counts, not these multiplied totals.
Pandava Allies and Contingents: The Udyoga Parva lists the Pandava contingents that made up seven akshauhinis; commonly cited single-akshauhini contributors include Satyaki (Yuyudhana) of the Vrishnis, Dhrishtaketu of Chedi, Jayatsena son of Jarasandha of Magadha, the Pandya king, Drupada of Panchala and Virata of Matsya — exact attributions vary between editions and translations.

Panchala under King Drupada provided the core of the Pandava army; its leaders included Drupada's sons Dhrishtadyumna and Shikhandi and the Panchala princes Yudhamanyu, Uttamaujas and Satyajit (whose exact kinship to Drupada is given differently in different passages and translations).
Matsya under King Virata fought for the Pandavas with his sons Uttara (Uttara Kumara), Shveta and Shankha.

Other Pandava-side warriors include the five Kekaya brothers (exiled Kekaya princes), Chekitana of the Vrishnis, Kuntibhoja and Purujit (Kunti's adoptive kin), Shaibya, the king of Kashi, and Dhrishtaketu of Chedi (son of Shishupala).

Family fighters on the Pandava side included Abhimanyu (Arjuna's son by Subhadra), the five Upapandavas (Draupadi's sons), Ghatotkacha (Bhima's son by the rakshasi Hidimbi) and Iravan (Arjuna's son by the Naga princess Ulupi).
Yuyutsu, Dhritarashtra's son by a vaishya maid, crossed from the Kaurava side to the Pandavas on the first morning.
Krishna fought for the Pandavas only as Arjuna's charioteer and counsellor, having pledged not to take up weapons.
Kaurava Allies and Contingents: The Udyoga Parva attributes roughly one akshauhini each to Bhagadatta of Pragjyotisha (with Chinas and Kiratas), Bhurishravas, Shalya of Madra, Kritavarma of the Bhojas, Jayadratha of Sindhu-Sauvira, Sudakshina of Kamboja (with Yavanas and Shakas), Nila of Mahishmati, Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti (each with an akshauhini in some readings), and the Kekaya brothers allied to Duryodhana; with the forces of other kings and Duryodhana's own these make eleven — exact counts per king vary between editions.
Gandhara under Shakuni, Duryodhana's maternal uncle, fought for the Kauravas; Shakuni's son Uluka also fought.
The Trigartas under Susharma and his brothers led the Samshaptakas, warriors sworn to kill Arjuna or die, who repeatedly drew Arjuna away from the main battle.
The Narayani army of Krishna's gopa warriors fought for Duryodhana and joined the Samshaptakas against Arjuna in the Drona Parva.
Bahlika (Shantanu's elder brother, an aged Kuru), his son Somadatta and grandson Bhurishravas fought on the Kaurava side.
Kalinga forces fought for the Kauravas and were heavily defeated by Bhima on day 2.
Rakshasa allies of the Kauravas included Alambusha and Alayudha, both killed during the war.
Drona, Kripa and Ashwatthama — the Kuru preceptors and Drona's son — fought for the Kauravas out of obligation to the Hastinapura throne.
Dhritarashtra's hundred sons, led by Duryodhana and Duhshasana, fought for the Kauravas; Vikarna, who had protested Draupadi's treatment, still fought and died for his brothers.
Pandava Command Structure: Yudhishthira chose seven commanders, one for each Pandava akshauhini: Drupada, Virata, Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandi, Satyaki, Chekitana and Bhima.
Pandava akshauhini commanders (7): Drupada | Virata | Dhrishtadyumna | Shikhandi | Satyaki | Chekitana | Bhima.
For supreme commander, the brothers proposed different leaders: Sahadeva named Virata, Nakula named Drupada, Bhima named Shikhandi, and Arjuna named Dhrishtadyumna; Krishna endorsed Dhrishtadyumna.
Dhrishtadyumna, Drupada's son born from the sacrificial fire to kill Drona, served as Pandava supreme commander (senapati) for all eighteen days.
The text also places Arjuna over the commanders, with Krishna as Arjuna's guide and charioteer.
Pandava supreme commander by days: Dhrishtadyumna 18.
Kaurava Command Structure: Duryodhana appointed Bhishma supreme commander (the Bhishmabhishechana, 'Consecration of Bhishma'), with eleven akshauhini commanders under him.

The eleven Kaurava akshauhini commanders are commonly listed as: Kripa, Drona, Shalya, Jayadratha, Sudakshina, Kritavarma, Ashwatthama, Karna, Bhurishravas, Shakuni and Bahlika (lists vary slightly between editions).
Bhishma accepted command on two conditions: he would not kill the Pandavas themselves, and either he or Karna must fight first; Karna vowed not to fight while Bhishma lived.
Bhishma promised Duryodhana to slay ten thousand warriors every day of his command.
Kaurava supreme commanders by days of war: Bhishma 1–10 | Drona 11–15 | Karna 16–17 | Shalya 18.
Kaurava supreme command, number of days held: Bhishma 10 | Drona 5 | Karna 2 | Shalya 1.
After Shalya's death on day 18 and Duryodhana's defeat, the dying Duryodhana anointed Ashwatthama as commander for the night, leading to the night massacre (Sauptika Parva).
Karna entered the battle only on day 11, after Bhishma's fall, serving under Drona before becoming commander on day 16.
Warrior Rankings — Rathas and Atirathas: In the Rathatirathasankhya ('Counting of Rathas and Atirathas') of the Udyoga Parva, Bhishma rated the warriors of both armies by fighting strength.

Ranks of chariot-warriors used in the epic: ardharatha (half a ratha), ratha, atiratha and maharatha; precise definitions such as how many opponents each could face come from later commentarial glosses and vary.

Bhishma rated Karna only an ardharatha (half-warrior), citing his loss of his natural armour and earrings, Parashurama's curse and his boastfulness; Karna, enraged, swore not to fight while Bhishma commanded.
Bhishma told Duryodhana he would not fight Shikhandi because Shikhandi had been born female, and narrated the story of Amba (the Ambopakhyana) to explain why.
Asked how long each could destroy the Pandava army alone, Bhishma said one month, Drona one month, Kripa two months, Ashwatthama ten nights and Karna five days (Udyoga Parva).
Claimed time to destroy the Pandava army alone, in days (a month taken as 30 days): Bhishma 30 | Drona 30 | Kripa 60 | Ashwatthama 10 | Karna 5.

When Yudhishthira asked the same of Arjuna, Arjuna replied that with Krishna as his ally he could destroy all three worlds in an instant using Shiva's Pashupata weapon, but would not use it on ordinary men.
Neutrals, Defectors and Divided Loyaltie: Balarama refused to fight for either side because both were dear to him, and spent the war on a pilgrimage along the Sarasvati, returning for the final mace duel.
Rukmi offered his akshauhini to both sides and was refused by both because of his boasting, so he sat out the war.
Yuyutsu was the only son of Dhritarashtra to fight for the Pandavas, and the only one to survive the war.
Shalya, the Pandava twins' maternal uncle, was won over to the Kaurava side by Duryodhana's hospitality but secretly promised to undermine Karna.
Bhishma, Drona and Kripa fought for the Kauravas despite favouring the Pandavas, explaining to Yudhishthira that they were bound by the Kauravas' wealth and patronage.
Vidura did not fight in the war; the story that he broke his bow in protest so as not to take part comes from later and regional retellings, not the Critical Edition.
The Yadavas were split: Krishna (non-combatant) and Satyaki with the Pandavas; Kritavarma and the Narayani army with the Kauravas.
Karna, Kunti's eldest son, fought against his half-brothers out of loyalty to Duryodhana.
Banners, Conches and Chariots: At the opening of the Bhagavad Gita, Bhishma blew his conch first with a sound like a lion's roar, signalling the start of hostilities.
Named conches blown at the start of the Gita (Chapter 1): Krishna Panchajanya | Arjuna Devadatta | Bhima Paundra | Yudhishthira Anantavijaya | Nakula Sughosha | Sahadeva Manipushpaka.
Arjuna's chariot banner bore an ape (kapidhvaja); the Vana Parva has Hanuman promise Bhima that he would roar from Arjuna's banner, and later tradition identifies the ape as Hanuman.
Bhishma's banner bore a golden palm tree (tala), as described in the Bhishma Parva.

Banner emblems as described in the Drona Parva (descriptions vary by edition): Drona a golden altar (vedi) | Karna an elephant's girth-rope | Ashwatthama a lion's tail | Kripa a bull | Shalya a ploughshare | Jayadratha a boar | Bhurishravas a sacrificial post (yupa).
Krishna's own chariot was driven by his charioteer Daruka; at Kurukshetra Krishna drove Arjuna's chariot, which had been a gift from Agni at the Khandava burning.
Bhima's charioteer was Vishoka; Shalya served as Karna's charioteer on day 17.
Sanjaya, Dhritarashtra's charioteer, received divine vision from Vyasa so he could see and narrate the whole battle to the blind king.
Encampments and the Battlefield: The war was fought at Kurukshetra, called Dharmakshetra ('field of dharma') in the first verse of the Bhagavad Gita; Kurukshetra is traditionally identified with the region around modern Kurukshetra in Haryana.
Part of Kurukshetra is called Samantapanchaka, said to be where Parashurama filled five lakes with the blood of kshatriyas; the final mace duel was fought there.
The Pandavas marched from Upaplavya and encamped on level ground at Kurukshetra near the Hiranvati river, according to the Udyoga Parva, where a protective moat was dug around the camp.
Vyasa offered Dhritarashtra sight to watch the battle; Dhritarashtra declined, not wishing to see his kin killed, so Vyasa gave Sanjaya divine vision to see and report everything.
Before battle Vyasa described terrible omens to Dhritarashtra — portents in the sky and nature foretelling great slaughter (Bhishma Parva).
The Bhishma Parva opens with a geographical digression (Jambukhanda and Bhumi sub-parvas) in which Sanjaya describes the world, before the battle narrative begins.

Setting and Narrative Frame: The Bhagavad Gita ('Song of the Lord') is a dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna on Arjuna's chariot between the two armies at Kurukshetra, just before the first day's fighting.
The Gita forms chapters 23–40 of the Bhishma Parva in the Critical Edition (chapters 25–42 in the vulgate numbering), within the Bhagavadgita sub-parva.
The Gita is framed as Sanjaya's narration to the blind Dhritarashtra; Sanjaya returns to Dhritarashtra after Bhishma's fall on day 10 and then recounts the war from the start, including the Gita.
The Gita opens with Dhritarashtra's only verse, asking Sanjaya what his sons and the Pandavas did on the field of dharma, Kurukshetra.
In Chapter 1, Duryodhana surveys both armies and lists their champions to Drona; Bhishma blows his conch, and conches sound on both sides.
Arjuna asks Krishna to drive the chariot between the armies, sees teachers, grandfathers, uncles, cousins and friends arrayed to fight, and collapses in grief, laying down his bow.

Krishna's teaching moves from rebuking Arjuna's despondency, through the immortality of the self and selfless action, to devotion and the revelation of his cosmic form; Arjuna ends by declaring his doubts gone and his resolve restored.
Gita Jayanti, the modern festival of the Gita's 'birthday', is observed on Margashirsha Shukla Ekadashi (Mokshada Ekadashi); this date reflects later tradition, not a statement in the epic.
Verse Counts per Chapter: The common vulgate Bhagavad Gita, the text commented on by Shankara, has 18 chapters and 700 verses.

Gita verses per chapter (700-verse vulgate): Ch1 47 | Ch2 72 | Ch3 43 | Ch4 42 | Ch5 29 | Ch6 47 | Ch7 30 | Ch8 28 | Ch9 34 | Ch10 42 | Ch11 55 | Ch12 20 | Ch13 34 | Ch14 27 | Ch15 20 | Ch16 24 | Ch17 28 | Ch18 78.
Longest Gita chapters by verses: Ch18 78 | Ch2 72 | Ch11 55 | Ch1 47 | Ch6 47.
Shortest Gita chapters by verses: Ch12 20 | Ch15 20 | Ch16 24 | Ch14 27 | Ch8 28 | Ch17 28.

Some editions (e.g. many popular printings) add an extra opening verse to Chapter 13 in which Arjuna asks about prakriti, purusha, the field and the knower of the field, giving 35 verses for Chapter 13 and 701 in total; Shankara's text does not count it.
Gita verses by group of six chapters (700-verse vulgate): Ch1–6 280 | Ch7–12 209 | Ch13–18 211.

Traditional readings divide the Gita into three hexads: chapters 1–6 emphasising karma (action), 7–12 bhakti (devotion), and 13–18 jnana (knowledge) — a later interpretive scheme, not a division in the text.
Chapter Titles — Chapters 1 to 6: Chapter titles come from the colophons of manuscripts and printed editions; the wording varies between editions, and the Critical Edition does not include the colophons as part of the text.
Gita Chapter 1 — Arjuna Vishada Yoga (Arjuna's Despondency): Arjuna sees his kin in both armies and refuses to fight.
Gita Chapter 2 — Sankhya Yoga (Yoga of Knowledge/Discernment): the immortal self, duty, and the steady-minded sage (sthitaprajna).
Gita Chapter 3 — Karma Yoga (Yoga of Action): why action is unavoidable and should be done as sacrifice, without attachment.
Gita Chapter 4 — Jnana Karma Sannyasa Yoga (Knowledge and Renunciation of Action; also called Jnana Yoga): Krishna's repeated descents to restore dharma and action burned clean by knowledge.
Gita Chapter 5 — Karma Sannyasa Yoga (Renunciation of Action): renunciation and disciplined action lead to the same goal.
Gita Chapter 6 — Atma Samyama Yoga or Dhyana Yoga (Self-Discipline/Meditation): the practice of meditation and the balanced yogi.
Chapter Titles — Chapters 7 to 12: Gita Chapter 7 — Jnana Vijnana Yoga (Knowledge and Realisation): Krishna's lower and higher natures and the kinds of devotees.
Gita Chapter 8 — Akshara Brahma Yoga (the Imperishable Brahman): death, remembrance of God at the end, and the paths of departure.
Gita Chapter 9 — Raja Vidya Raja Guhya Yoga (Royal Knowledge, Royal Secret): God pervades all; even a leaf, flower, fruit or water offered with devotion is accepted.
Gita Chapter 10 — Vibhuti Yoga (Divine Manifestations): Krishna lists his glories as the best in every class of beings and things.
Gita Chapter 11 — Vishvarupa Darshana Yoga (Vision of the Universal Form): Arjuna, granted divine sight, sees Krishna's cosmic form devouring the warriors as Time.
Gita Chapter 12 — Bhakti Yoga (Yoga of Devotion): devotion to the personal God and the qualities of the devotee dear to Krishna.
Chapter Titles — Chapters 13 to 18: Gita Chapter 13 — Kshetra Kshetrajna Vibhaga Yoga (the Field and the Knower of the Field; also Prakriti Purusha Viveka Yoga): body as field, self as knower, matter and spirit.
Gita Chapter 14 — Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga (the Three Gunas): sattva, rajas and tamas and how to transcend them.
Gita Chapter 15 — Purushottama Yoga (the Supreme Person): the inverted ashvattha tree of worldly existence and the supreme being beyond perishable and imperishable.
Gita Chapter 16 — Daivasura Sampad Vibhaga Yoga (Divine and Demonic Qualities): virtues that liberate and vices — lust, anger, greed — that bind.
Gita Chapter 17 — Shraddhatraya Vibhaga Yoga (Three Kinds of Faith): faith, food, sacrifice, austerity and charity classified by the gunas; the formula Om Tat Sat.
Gita Chapter 18 — Moksha Sannyasa Yoga (Liberation through Renunciation): renunciation of fruits, duty by one's nature (svadharma), and the final call to surrender to Krishna.
Speakers and Verse Distribution: The 700 Gita verses are commonly divided among four speakers.
Gita verses by speaker (700-verse vulgate, common count; some tallies differ by a verse or two): Krishna 574 | Arjuna 84 | Sanjaya 41 | Dhritarashtra 1.
Krishna speaks about 82 percent of the 700-verse Gita.
A verse found in some manuscripts after the Gita (in the vulgate Bhishma Parva, not accepted in the Critical Edition) claims a 745-verse Gita.
Speaker counts in the 745-verse claim (manuscript tradition): Krishna 620 | Arjuna 57 | Sanjaya 67 | Dhritarashtra 1.
Dhritarashtra speaks only the opening verse; Sanjaya's verses frame the dialogue and close the Gita with his wonder at what he witnessed.
Core Themes — Dharma, Duty and Action: Arjuna's crisis in the Gita is a conflict of dharmas: his kshatriya duty to fight a just war versus his duty to family, teachers and the social order.
Svadharma, one's own duty according to one's nature and station, is better performed imperfectly than another's duty performed well — a teaching stated in both Chapter 3 and Chapter 18.
Nishkama karma — action without craving for its fruits — is the Gita's central ethical idea: one has a right to the action, never to its results (Chapter 2).
Karma yoga teaches that action performed as an offering, free of egoism and attachment, does not bind the doer.
Krishna argues that inaction is impossible for embodied beings and that withdrawing from duty out of fear or grief is not true renunciation.
Loka-sangraha, acting to hold the world together and set an example, is given as a reason for even the enlightened to act (Chapter 3).
The Gita does not resolve the morality of war simply: interpreters have read its battlefield as literal duty, as an allegory of the inner struggle, or as both.
Core Themes — Self, Knowledge and Devoti: The atman (self) in the Gita is eternal and unborn; it is not slain when the body is slain, and it changes bodies as a person changes clothes (Chapter 2, paraphrased).
Sthitaprajna, the person of steady wisdom, remains even-minded in pleasure and pain, success and failure (Chapter 2).
The Gita synthesises several paths: karma yoga (action), jnana yoga (knowledge), dhyana yoga (meditation) and bhakti yoga (devotion).
The three gunas — sattva (clarity), rajas (passion) and tamas (inertia) — classify nature, faith, food, actions and temperaments in Chapters 14, 17 and 18.
Krishna presents himself as the supreme God who descends age after age whenever dharma declines, to protect the good and restore righteousness (Chapter 4, paraphrased).
In Chapter 11 Krishna reveals himself as all-consuming Time, telling Arjuna that the warriors are already slain by him and Arjuna is only the instrument.
The Gita's final teaching (Chapter 18) asks Arjuna to give up all dharmas and take refuge in Krishna alone, promising release from all sin — a verse read differently by different schools.
Famous Verses and Their Reception: Gita 2.47, on having a right to action but not its fruits, is the most cited statement of nishkama karma (paraphrased here, not quoted).
Gita 4.7–8, on Krishna's descent whenever dharma declines, is the classic scriptural basis for the doctrine of avatars.

Gita 11.32, in which Krishna declares himself Time grown mighty to destroy the worlds, was recalled by J. Robert Oppenheimer in connection with the first atomic test in 1945, in his own English rendering.
Gita 18.66, the call to abandon all dharmas and take refuge in Krishna, is called the 'charama shloka' (final verse) in the Shri Vaishnava tradition of Ramanuja.
Gita 2.20, on the self that is never born and never dies, has a close parallel in the Katha Upanishad, reflecting the Gita's debt to the Upanishads.
The Gita's closing verse has Sanjaya declare that wherever Krishna, lord of yoga, and Arjuna the archer are, there will be fortune, victory and righteousness (paraphrased).
Text, Recensions and Dating: The 700-verse Gita is remarkably stable across most manuscripts compared with the rest of the Mahabharata, partly because Shankara's commentary fixed its text early.

The Kashmiri recension of the Gita, studied by F. Otto Schrader (1930), contains a number of additional verses and half-verses and many variant readings; Abhinavagupta's commentary (Gitartha-sangraha) follows this recension. Reported extra-verse counts vary by manuscript and are roughly a dozen or so.
The Bhishma Parva of the BORI Critical Edition, including the Gita, was edited by S. K. Belvalkar (1940s); the Critical Edition gives 700 verses and relegates the 745-verse claim to the apparatus.

Most modern scholars date the Gita's composition to the last centuries BCE or around the turn of the era; estimates range roughly from the 5th century BCE to the 2nd century CE, and many see it as layered.
Some scholars (e.g. Rudolf Otto, Richard Garbe) argued for an original core with later theistic or philosophical additions; others defend its unity — the question is unresolved.

Traditional belief holds that the Gita was spoken on the battlefield in the time it took for armies to stand ready, and that Sanjaya witnessed it through Vyasa's gift of divine sight; historians regard the dialogue as a literary composition.
Commentaries and Influence: Shankara (c. 8th century CE) wrote the oldest surviving full commentary on the Gita, from the Advaita (non-dual) Vedanta standpoint, stressing knowledge as the path to liberation.
Ramanuja (c. 11th–12th century) commented from Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism), emphasising devotion and surrender to Vishnu-Narayana.
Madhva (c. 13th century) commented from Dvaita (dualism), stressing the eternal distinction between God and souls.
Jnaneshwar (Dnyaneshwar) composed the Jnaneshwari (c. 1290 CE), a celebrated Marathi verse commentary on the Gita.

Bal Gangadhar Tilak's Gita Rahasya (published 1915, written in Mandalay jail) read the Gita as a gospel of energetic action (karma yoga); Mahatma Gandhi called it his 'mother' and wrote Anasakti Yoga (Gujarati, completed 1929, published 1930), reading it as a teaching of selfless non-attachment and, allegorically, of inner struggle.
Sri Aurobindo's Essays on the Gita (serialised 1916–1920) and Swami Vivekananda's lectures popularised it in modern Hindu thought.
Charles Wilkins published the first English translation of the Gita in 1785; Edwin Arnold's verse translation The Song Celestial appeared in 1885.
Major Gita commentators by approximate century CE (Abhinavagupta's life spans the 10th–11th, Ramanuja's the 11th–12th): Shankara 8 | Abhinavagupta 10 | Ramanuja 11 | Madhva 13 | Jnaneshwar 13.
The Gita Within the Epic — Anugita and O: In the Ashvamedhika Parva, after the war, Arjuna admits he has forgotten the teaching, and Krishna gives a second discourse known as the Anugita ('After-Gita').
The Mahabharata contains other teaching dialogues sometimes called gitas, such as the Vyadha Gita (Vana Parva) and many discourses in the Shanti Parva.
Within the epic's plot, the Gita's immediate effect is that Arjuna takes up his bow; Yudhishthira then seeks the elders' blessings and the battle begins.
The universal form shown in Gita Chapter 11 echoes the vishvarupa Krishna displayed in the Kuru court during his peace mission (Udyoga Parva).
The Gita's location in the Bhishma Parva means it is narrated after the outcome of Bhishma's command is already known to Dhritarashtra.

War Overview and Timeline Tables: The Kurukshetra war lasted eighteen days, followed on the night of the eighteenth day by Ashwatthama's massacre of the sleeping Pandava camp.
Days of war narrated in each parva: Bhishma Parva 10 | Drona Parva 5 | Karna Parva 2 | Shalya Parva 1.
Parva coverage of the war: Bhishma Parva days 1–10 | Drona Parva days 11–15 | Karna Parva days 16–17 | Shalya Parva day 18 | Sauptika Parva night after day 18.
Kaurava supreme commanders by days: Bhishma 1–10 | Drona 11–15 | Karna 16–17 | Shalya 18 | Ashwatthama night after 18 (appointed by the dying Duryodhana).
Pandava supreme commander: Dhrishtadyumna for all eighteen days, until he was killed in the night massacre.

Major turning points by day: Day 10 fall of Bhishma | Day 13 death of Abhimanyu | Day 14 death of Jayadratha and night death of Ghatotkacha | Day 15 death of Drona | Day 17 death of Karna | Day 18 deaths of Shalya and Shakuni and Duryodhana's defeat.
Fighting was meant to stop at sunset each day, but the battle continued through the night of day 14 into day 15, and the war ended with the night raid after day 18.
Days 1–3 — Opening Battles: Day 1: After the Gita and Yudhishthira's visit to the elders, Yuyutsu crossed to the Pandava side; the Kauravas under Bhishma dominated the first day.

Day 1: Virata's son Uttara (Uttara Kumara) was killed by Shalya, and Virata's son Shveta was killed by Bhishma; the young Abhimanyu fought Bhishma boldly. The Pandava array that day was the Vajra ('thunderbolt') formation arranged by Arjuna.
Day 1 ended with the Pandavas dispirited by Bhishma's power; Yudhishthira was anxious and Krishna reassured him.
Day 2: The Pandavas formed the Krauncha (heron/crane) array; Arjuna checked Bhishma, and Dhrishtadyumna fought Drona.
Day 2: Bhima destroyed the Kalinga contingent, killing the Kalinga king (Shrutayu in many translations) and princes including Shakradeva and Bhanumat; the day went in the Pandavas' favour.
Day 3: Bhishma arrayed the Kauravas in the Garuda (eagle) formation and the Pandavas answered with the Ardhachandra (half-moon) formation.
Day 3: Bhima struck Duryodhana unconscious with an arrow; Duryodhana later accused Bhishma of favouring the Pandavas, and Bhishma fought more fiercely.

Day 3: Angered by Arjuna's mildness towards Bhishma, Krishna leapt from the chariot to attack Bhishma himself, about to break his vow not to bear arms; Arjuna caught him and promised to fight in earnest. In the Sanskrit text Krishna raises his discus (Sudarshana); many popular retellings substitute a chariot wheel; a similar charge recurs on day 9.
Days 4–6 — Bhima's Rampage and Shifting: Day 4: Bhima killed eight of Dhritarashtra's sons; Ghatotkacha routed Kaurava forces, and Abhimanyu fought with distinction.
After day 4 in the text: Duryodhana asked Bhishma why the Pandavas could not be beaten, and Bhishma explained Krishna's divinity and the Pandavas' righteousness, urging peace (refused).
Day 5: Bhishma formed the Makara (crocodile/sea-monster) array and the Pandavas the Shyena (hawk) array.
Day 5: Bhurishravas killed the ten sons of Satyaki in a single engagement.
Day 6: The Pandavas formed the Makara array and the Kauravas the Krauncha array; Drona caused heavy losses.
Day 6: Bhima plunged deep into the Kaurava ranks on foot; Dhrishtadyumna rescued him, in the text stupefying the Kauravas with a bewildering weapon (pramohana), which Drona neutralised.
Day 6: Bhima wounded Duryodhana badly; the day ended with heavy losses on both sides.
Days 7–9 — Iravan's Death and Bhishma Un: Day 7: As commonly listed, the Kauravas formed the Mandala (circular) array and the Pandavas the Vajra array; many single combats took place, including Arjuna against the Trigartas and Ghatotkacha against Bhagadatta.
Day 8: Iravan, Arjuna's son by the Naga princess Ulupi, was killed by the rakshasa Alambusha after destroying many Kaurava horsemen; Arjuna grieved deeply.
Day 8: Bhima killed eight more of Dhritarashtra's sons; Ghatotkacha caused panic among the Kauravas.

Day 8 formations: the Pandava array is named Shringataka (three-horned) in translations; the Kaurava array is described as vast like the ocean, and some popular lists call it Kurma (tortoise) — names are uncertain.
Day 9: Bhishma arrayed the Kauravas in the Sarvatobhadra ('auspicious on all sides') formation and caused enormous slaughter among the Pandava forces.

Day 9: Krishna again leapt down to attack Bhishma, this time with only his horse-whip in hand in the Sanskrit text; Bhishma welcomed death at his hands, and Arjuna restrained Krishna and renewed his vow to fight.
Night of day 9: The Pandavas and Krishna visited Bhishma in his tent; Bhishma told them he would not fight Shikhandi, who had been born female, and advised them to place Shikhandi before Arjuna.
Day 10 — The Fall of Bhishma: Day 10: Arjuna advanced with Shikhandi in front of his chariot; Bhishma refused to strike Shikhandi and was pierced by Arjuna's arrows from behind Shikhandi.
Day 10: Bhishma fell from his chariot near sunset, his body held off the ground by the arrows piercing it — the bed of arrows (shara-shayya).
Day 10: Fighting stopped as warriors of both sides gathered around the fallen Bhishma; Arjuna made him a pillow of three arrows when he asked for one fit for a warrior.
The next morning, when Bhishma asked for water, Arjuna shot an arrow into the earth and a stream of pure water sprang up for him to drink.
Bhishma had a boon from his father Shantanu to choose the time of his death; he chose to wait on the bed of arrows until the sun's northward course (uttarayana).
Karna visited the fallen Bhishma, who told him he had always known Karna was Kunti's son and urged reconciliation; Karna sought his blessing to fight and entered battle the next day.
With Bhishma's fall, Sanjaya returned to Dhritarashtra and began his narration of the war (Bhishma Parva).
Days 11–12 — Drona Takes Command: Day 11: Drona became Kaurava commander and promised Duryodhana he would capture Yudhishthira alive, provided Arjuna could be kept away.
Day 11: Drona arrayed the Kauravas in the Shakata (cart) formation according to common lists, and the Pandavas used the Krauncha formation; Arjuna's presence foiled Drona's attempt on Yudhishthira.
Day 11: Karna fought for the first time in the war.
Day 12: The Samshaptakas, led by Susharma of Trigarta, swore to conquer or die and challenged Arjuna, drawing him to the south of the field.
Day 12: The Panchala prince Satyajit, left to guard Yudhishthira, was killed by Drona; Yudhishthira escaped capture.

Day 12: Arjuna killed Bhagadatta of Pragjyotisha and his great elephant Supratika; Bhagadatta's Vaishnava weapon, hurled at Arjuna, was received by Krishna on his chest, where it became a garland (Vaijayanti).
Day 12 formations are given as Garuda (Kaurava) and Ardhachandra (Pandava) in some popular lists; the text's naming is less certain.
Day 13 — The Chakravyuha and Abhimanyu: Day 13: With Arjuna again drawn away by the Samshaptakas, Drona formed the Chakravyuha (wheel/discus array), which among the Pandavas only Arjuna, Krishna, Pradyumna and Abhimanyu could penetrate; Abhimanyu knew how to enter but not how to exit.

Day 13: Abhimanyu broke into the Chakravyuha, but Jayadratha, using a boon from Shiva to hold back all the Pandavas except Arjuna for one day, sealed the breach so Bhima, Yudhishthira and the others could not follow.
Day 13: Inside the array Abhimanyu killed many warriors, including Duryodhana's son Lakshmana and Brihadbala of Kosala.

Day 13: Several great warriors attacked Abhimanyu together — commonly listed as Drona, Kripa, Karna, Ashwatthama, Brihadbala and Kritavarma; on Drona's advice Karna cut his bow, and his horses and charioteer were killed.

Day 13: Fighting on with sword, chariot wheel and mace, Abhimanyu was finally killed by the son of Duhshasana, who struck him on the head with a mace as Abhimanyu was rising from the ground after both had fallen.
Day 13 evening: Learning of Abhimanyu's death, Arjuna vowed to kill Jayadratha before sunset the next day or enter fire himself.

The popular story that Abhimanyu learned to enter the Chakravyuha while in his mother Subhadra's womb, hearing Arjuna describe it, is a later or popular addition; in the Sanskrit epic Abhimanyu says Arjuna taught him how to break in.
Some retellings call the day-13 array Padmavyuha (lotus array); the epic names it Chakravyuha.
Day 14 and Its Night — Jayadratha and Gh: Day 14: Drona formed a combined array — a Shakata (cart) array in front and a Padma (lotus) array behind with a Suchi (needle) array within it — and placed Jayadratha deep at the rear.
Day 14: Arjuna fought through the front of Drona's array towards Jayadratha; Yudhishthira sent Satyaki and then Bhima after him.

Day 14: Bhurishravas was about to kill the exhausted Satyaki when Arjuna, urged by Krishna, cut off Bhurishravas's arm; Bhurishravas sat down to fast unto death and Satyaki beheaded him, an act condemned by onlookers.
Day 14: Bhima killed many of Dhritarashtra's sons, including Vikarna, whom he respected for having defended Draupadi.

Day 14: Just before sunset Arjuna killed Jayadratha; many versions say Krishna created a darkness (in popular retellings by covering the sun with his discus) so that Jayadratha came out of hiding — accounts differ between recensions.

Day 14: Arjuna's arrows carried Jayadratha's head into the lap of his father Vriddhakshatra, who had decreed that whoever made his son's head fall to the earth would have his own head shatter; when the startled father let it fall, his own head burst (details vary between versions).
Night of day 14: The battle continued by torchlight; Ghatotkacha, powerful at night, devastated the Kauravas, and Duryodhana begged Karna to stop him.
Night of day 14: Karna used Indra's one-time spear (the Vasavi Shakti), saved for Arjuna, to kill Ghatotkacha; Krishna rejoiced because Arjuna was now safe from it.
Day 15 — The Death of Drona: Day 15: In the early fighting Drona killed his old enemy Drupada and also King Virata.
Day 15: Drona used the Brahmastra against ordinary soldiers; sages appeared and rebuked him for using celestial weapons on those who did not know them, and urged him to lay down arms.
Day 15: On Krishna's advice Bhima killed an elephant named Ashwatthama (belonging to King Indravarman of Malava) and announced that Ashwatthama was dead.

Day 15: Drona asked Yudhishthira, known for truthfulness; Yudhishthira said Ashwatthama was dead, adding indistinctly that it was an elephant; his chariot, which had always moved four fingers above the ground, then touched the earth.
Day 15: Grief-stricken, Drona laid down his weapons and sat in yogic meditation; Dhrishtadyumna beheaded him despite Arjuna's protests.

Day 15: Enraged at his father's death, Ashwatthama released the Narayanastra; Krishna told the Pandava army to dismount and lay down arms, and the weapon subsided; Bhima resisted until he was forced down.
Day 15: Arjuna and Satyaki condemned Dhrishtadyumna's act and a bitter quarrel broke out in the Pandava camp; Ashwatthama's other weapons were countered by Arjuna.
Popular retellings say Krishna had conches and drums sounded to drown out Yudhishthira's word 'elephant'; the Sanskrit text says Yudhishthira spoke it indistinctly.
Day 16 — Karna's First Day as Commander: Day 16: Karna became Kaurava commander and arrayed the army in the Makara formation; the Pandavas answered with the Ardhachandra (half-moon) formation.
Day 16: Ashwatthama killed the Pandya king, a leading Pandava ally.
Day 16: Karna defeated Nakula but spared him, honouring his promise to Kunti not to kill any Pandava except Arjuna.
Day 16: Arjuna again fought the Samshaptakas while Bhima, Satyaki and Dhrishtadyumna fought Karna's divisions.
Day 16 evening: Karna asked Duryodhana to make Shalya, an expert charioteer equal to Krishna, his charioteer for the decisive duel with Arjuna.
Day 17 — The Death of Karna: Day 17: Shalya agreed to drive Karna's chariot on condition that he could speak as he pleased, and spent the day belittling Karna, including telling him the parable of a crow who boasted against swans.
Day 17: Karna defeated and wounded Yudhishthira, sparing him; Yudhishthira, in pain, taunted Arjuna and told him to give his Gandiva bow to someone else.

Day 17: Arjuna drew his sword to kill Yudhishthira, having vowed to kill anyone who told him to give up the Gandiva; Krishna intervened with stories about truth and intention, and Arjuna instead spoke harshly to his brother, then wanted to kill himself, until Krishna resolved the crisis.
Day 17: Bhima killed Duhshasana and fulfilled the vow he made at the dice game to drink his blood, horrifying onlookers.
Day 17: Arjuna killed Karna's son Vrishasena in front of Karna, avenging Abhimanyu.
Day 17: In the duel, Karna fired the serpent arrow (the Naga Ashvasena, a survivor of the Khandava fire); Krishna pressed the chariot into the earth so the arrow only struck off Arjuna's diadem.
Day 17: Karna's chariot wheel sank into the earth and he forgot the incantation for the Brahmastra, fulfilling two curses; he appealed to the rules of fair fighting while freeing his wheel.
Day 17: Krishna reminded Karna of his part in Draupadi's humiliation, the dice game and Abhimanyu's death, and Arjuna killed Karna with the Anjalika arrow; the Kaurava army fled in panic.
Day 18 — Shalya, Shakuni and Duryodhana: Day 18: Shalya became Kaurava commander and arrayed the remaining army, by common accounts in the Sarvatobhadra formation; the Pandavas attacked in three divisions.
Day 18: Yudhishthira killed Shalya with a spear (shakti) around midday — the most notable kill credited to the eldest Pandava.
Day 18: Sahadeva killed Shakuni, the instigator of the dice game, and his son Uluka.
Day 18: Bhima killed the last surviving sons of Dhritarashtra, leaving Duryodhana alone; Satyaki captured Sanjaya, who was released at Vyasa's request.
Day 18: Duryodhana fled and hid in the Dvaipayana lake, solidifying the waters by magic; hunters told Bhima where he was hiding.
Day 18: Yudhishthira offered Duryodhana the kingdom if he could defeat any one Pandava with a weapon of his choice — a rash offer Krishna criticised; Duryodhana chose the mace and fought Bhima.

Day 18: Balarama returned from his pilgrimage and the duel moved to Samantapanchaka; Bhima, on a signal from Arjuna who slapped his own thigh, broke Duryodhana's thighs, against the mace-fighting rule against blows below the navel.
Night after day 18: The dying Duryodhana appointed Ashwatthama commander, leading to the massacre of the sleeping Pandava camp.
The Night After Day 18 — Sauptika Massac: Ashwatthama, Kripa and Kritavarma — the last three Kaurava warriors — rested under a banyan tree, where Ashwatthama saw an owl killing sleeping crows and resolved to attack the Pandava camp at night.
Kripa argued against the night attack as unrighteous, but he and Kritavarma accompanied Ashwatthama.
At the camp gate Ashwatthama faced a terrifying guardian being; he offered himself to Shiva, who empowered him (Sauptika Parva).

Ashwatthama killed Dhrishtadyumna in his sleep by trampling and beating rather than by weapon, and then Shikhandi, Uttamaujas, Yudhamanyu and the five sons of Draupadi, among many Panchala and Matsya warriors.
Kripa and Kritavarma guarded the gates, killing those who fled, and set the camp on fire.
The five Pandavas, Krishna and Satyaki escaped because they were spending the night away from the camp.
Ashwatthama brought the news to Duryodhana, who died content that his enemies' sons were slain.
The night massacre is narrated in the Sauptika Parva, the tenth book of the Mahabharata.
Calendar, Dating and Recension Notes: The Udyoga Parva places Krishna's peace mission in the month called Kaumuda (usually identified with Kartika); Krishna told Karna the battle should begin at the new moon about seven days later.
Later Hindu tradition places the start of the war, and the Gita, in the month of Margashirsha, marked today by Gita Jayanti; this is traditional rather than textually exact.
Balarama, returning for the mace duel, says he had been on pilgrimage for 42 days, leaving under the Pushya asterism and returning under Shravana (Shalya Parva).
Bhishma says he has lain on the bed of arrows for 58 nights when he dies after the sun has turned north (uttarayana), according to the Anushasana Parva.
Time markers: War days 18 | Bhishma on arrow bed 58 nights | Balarama's pilgrimage 42 days | Years from war to Yadava destruction 36.

Indian tradition places the war at the junction of the Dvapara and Kali ages; the Kali Yuga's start is conventionally dated 3102 BCE, and some traditional reckonings put the war about 36 years earlier, with Kali beginning at Krishna's departure; astronomical attempts to date the war range from the 6th millennium BCE to the early 1st millennium BCE and remain disputed.

Mainstream historians regard the war as not securely datable; any historical core is often associated with the Kuru realm of the late Vedic period, while the epic was composed and expanded over centuries (c. 400 BCE–400 CE is a common estimate).
Formation names for many days are not given consistently across editions and translations; day-by-day tables of arrays in popular books are partly reconstructions.

Barbarika, the warrior whose severed head watched the whole war in popular legend (Khatu Shyam worship), does not appear in the Critical Edition; his story comes from the Skanda Purana and regional traditions.

What a Vyuha Is: A vyuha is a battle array: a named arrangement of chariots, elephants, cavalry and infantry, often shaped like an animal, bird, object or geometric figure.
Vyuha shapes in the Mahabharata served to protect the commander and key warriors, concentrate force at a point of attack, and let divisions support one another.
Each side usually announced a new array each morning, and the opposing commander chose a counter-array; the Kurukshetra narrative names many but not all of the daily arrays.
Vyuha terminology in Sanskrit military writing divides an array into a centre or chest (uras), flanks (kaksha), wings (paksha) and a reserve (pratigraha).
The Arthashastra (Book 10) describes four basic array types — danda (staff/line), bhoga (snake-like column), mandala (circle) and asamhata (dispersed) — with many sub-varieties.

The Manusmriti (chapter 7) mentions the danda, shakata (cart), varaha (boar), makara (sea-monster), suchi (needle), garuda (eagle) and padma (lotus) arrays, showing these names were part of a wider tradition.
Whether the epic's formations reflect real ancient tactics or a literary idealisation is debated; the descriptions are poetic and often lack practical detail.

Animal and Bird Formations: Krauncha vyuha, shaped like a heron or crane (sometimes rendered curlew), had a beak, head, neck, wings and tail, each held by named commanders; the Pandavas used it on day 2 and the Kauravas on day 6.
Garuda vyuha, shaped like the eagle mount of Vishnu, was used by Bhishma on day 3, with Bhishma at the beak; common lists also give it to Drona on day 12.
Makara vyuha, shaped like the makara, a crocodile-like sea creature, was used by the Kauravas on day 5, by the Pandavas on day 6 and by Karna on day 16.
Shyena vyuha, shaped like a hawk, was the Pandava answer to the Kaurava Makara array on day 5, with Bhima at its beak.
Kurma (tortoise) is given in some popular lists as the Kaurava array of day 8; the text's description of that day's array is less specific.
Animal arrays let a strong 'beak' or 'jaws' pierce the enemy while the 'wings' enveloped the flanks.
Geometric and Object Formations: Vajra vyuha, the thunderbolt array associated with Indra, was arranged by Arjuna for the Pandavas on day 1 as a compact, hard-to-break formation for a smaller army; it is also listed for the Pandavas on day 7.
Ardhachandra vyuha, a crescent or half-moon array that could envelop an attacker, was used by the Pandavas on day 3 against the Garuda array and on day 16 against Karna's Makara.
Mandala vyuha, a circular array offering defence on all sides, is listed for the Kauravas on day 7.

Sarvatobhadra vyuha ('auspicious/guarded on every side'), an all-round defensive array (often drawn as a square in modern diagrams), was used by Bhishma on day 9 and, by common accounts, by Shalya on day 18.
Shringataka vyuha, a horned or three-pointed array, is named for the Pandavas on day 8 in translations.
Shakata vyuha, a cart-shaped array with a broad front, was used by Drona on day 11 (common lists) and as the front portion of his day-14 array.
Suchi vyuha, the needle array, was a narrow, deep column used for penetration or, on day 14, to hide and protect Jayadratha inside Drona's Padma array.
Padma vyuha, the lotus array with concentric petals, formed the rear part of Drona's day-14 array; some popular retellings also use 'Padmavyuha' as another name for the day-13 Chakravyuha.
The Chakravyuha: The Chakravyuha (wheel or discus array) was formed by Drona on day 13 while Arjuna was drawn away by the Samshaptakas.

In the Drona Parva the Chakravyuha holds Duryodhana and leading Kaurava heroes within it, with Drona at its head; it is presented as very hard to penetrate and harder to leave, while the image of concentric, rotating rings comes mainly from later art and retellings.
In the epic, Abhimanyu says only Arjuna, Krishna, Pradyumna and he himself knew how to break into the Chakravyuha, and that he did not know how to come out.
The Pandava plan on day 13 was for Abhimanyu to open a breach and the others to follow; Jayadratha's boon from Shiva let him hold the breach against all the Pandavas except Arjuna.

The Chakravyuha's spiral or labyrinth shape in popular art and temple carvings (and the 'chakravyuha' as a metaphor for an inescapable trap) are later imaginative developments; the epic gives no precise geometric plan.
The story that Abhimanyu learned the Chakravyuha in his mother's womb is a popular addition not found in the Critical Edition narrative.
Drona's Day-14 Array — Shakata, Padma an: On day 14 Drona built a deep, layered array to protect Jayadratha from Arjuna's vow to kill him before sunset.
The front of Drona's day-14 array was a Shakata (cart) array, behind which lay a Padma (lotus) array, with a concealed Suchi (needle) array inside it where Jayadratha was stationed.
Drona himself stood at the head of the day-14 array, and Arjuna chose to go around him rather than spend the day fighting his teacher.
Kritavarma, Duryodhana, Karna, Ashwatthama, Kripa, Shalya, Bhurishravas and others guarded successive layers of the day-14 array.
Yudhishthira sent Satyaki and then Bhima into the array to support Arjuna, weakening the Pandava defence against Drona.
The day-14 array failed when Arjuna reached and killed Jayadratha just before sunset.
Rules of Engagement and Their Breaking: Before the battle the two sides agreed on rules of war, set out at the start of the Bhishma Parva.

Rules agreed before Kurukshetra included: fight only an equal (chariot against chariot, elephant against elephant, horse against horse, foot against foot); meet words with words; do not strike one who is retreating, has surrendered, is disarmed, unprepared or distracted; do not strike charioteers, draught animals, weapon-carriers or musicians.
Fighting was to take place between sunrise and sunset, with the armies mingling freely after the day's battle ended.

Breaches of the rules escalated through the war: the use of Shikhandi against Bhishma (day 10); many warriors attacking the lone Abhimanyu (day 13); Arjuna cutting off Bhurishravas's arm and Satyaki beheading him while he fasted (day 14); fighting through the night of day 14.

Further breaches included the elephant ruse and the killing of the meditating Drona (day 15); killing Karna while he freed his chariot wheel (day 17); Bhima's blow below the navel in the mace duel (day 18); and the massacre of sleeping warriors (night after day 18).
Both sides broke the rules: the Kauravas' assault on Abhimanyu and night massacre mirror the Pandavas' ruses against Bhishma, Drona, Karna and Duryodhana.
The text itself repeatedly voices criticism of these breaches through characters such as Arjuna, Balarama, Duryodhana and Kripa, making the war's fairness a central moral question of the epic.
Strategic Ploys — Pandava Side: Shikhandi as a shield (day 10): on Bhishma's own advice, Arjuna attacked from behind Shikhandi, whom Bhishma would not fight.
Ghatotkacha's night attack (night of day 14): Ghatotkacha's devastation forced Karna to use the one-time Vasavi Shakti he had saved for Arjuna.
The elephant ruse (day 15): Bhima killed an elephant named Ashwatthama so Drona would believe his son dead and lay down his arms.
Surrender to the Narayanastra (day 15): Krishna knew Ashwatthama's weapon would spare those who laid down arms, and ordered the army to dismount and submit.
Striking Karna when his wheel sank (day 17): Krishna urged Arjuna to kill Karna while he was struggling with his chariot wheel.
Matching Yudhishthira against Shalya (day 18): Krishna judged that Shalya should fall to Yudhishthira, who killed him with a spear.
The thigh signal (day 18): Krishna told Arjuna that Bhima could not win the mace duel fairly; Arjuna slapped his thigh to remind Bhima of his vow to break Duryodhana's thighs.
Strategic Ploys — Kaurava Side: The Samshaptakas: the Trigarta warriors and their allies swore to conquer or die, and repeatedly lured Arjuna away from the main battle, especially on days 12 and 13.
Drona's plan to capture Yudhishthira alive (days 11–12) aimed to end the war by forcing a second dice game or surrender; it failed whenever Arjuna returned.
Jayadratha's boon from Shiva was used to seal the Chakravyuha behind Abhimanyu on day 13, isolating him.
On day 14 Drona hid Jayadratha deep inside a layered Shakata–Padma–Suchi array to make Arjuna fail his vow and die by fire.
Karna saved Indra's Vasavi Shakti for Arjuna for days, until Duryodhana's panic at Ghatotkacha forced him to use it.
Bhishma's promise to kill ten thousand warriors a day and Drona's use of celestial weapons were meant to wear down the Pandava army by attrition.
After the defeat on day 18, Duryodhana hid in the Dvaipayana lake, and Ashwatthama's night raid tried to reverse the outcome by killing the Pandava camp in its sleep.
Celestial Weapons in the War: Astras are divine weapons invoked by mantra; in the epic they are given by gods or teachers and often cannot be recalled once released.
Vaishnavastra (day 12): Bhagadatta hurled it at Arjuna; Krishna took it on his chest, where it turned into the Vaijayanti garland.
Vasavi Shakti (night of day 14): Indra's spear, given to Karna in exchange for his natural armour and earrings, could be used only once; it killed Ghatotkacha.
Brahmastra (day 15): Drona used it on ordinary soldiers and was rebuked by sages; Arjuna also used Brahma weapons to counter Ashwatthama's attacks.
Narayanastra (day 15): Ashwatthama's weapon rained destruction on all who resisted; it subsided when the Pandava army laid down its arms.
Naga arrow (day 17): Karna's serpent arrow carrying the Naga Ashvasena struck off Arjuna's diadem after Krishna pressed the chariot down.
Varuna's mace: Shrutayudha had a mace from Varuna that would kill its wielder if hurled at a non-combatant; on day 14 he threw it at Krishna and it rebounded and killed him.

Brahmashiras (after the war): Ashwatthama and Arjuna released it against each other; Arjuna withdrew his, while Ashwatthama, unable to recall his, redirected it into the wombs of the Pandava women; Krishna promised to revive Uttara's unborn child (Sauptika Parva) and revived the stillborn Parikshit at his birth (Ashvamedhika Parva).
Command, Signals and the Rhythm of Battl: Conches signalled the start of battle and moments of triumph; Bhishma's conch opened the war and the Pandavas answered with theirs.
Each day's battle normally ended at sunset with the withdrawal of the armies (avahara), when warriors returned to their camps.
The night battle of day 14 was fought by the light of lamps and torches carried on chariots and by soldiers, as the Drona Parva describes.
Commanders were consecrated before taking office, as Bhishma was anointed in the Udyoga Parva and Drona, Karna and Shalya were appointed in turn after their predecessors fell.
Charioteers mattered tactically: Krishna's driving saved Arjuna from Karna's serpent arrow, and Shalya's taunts were meant to weaken Karna.
Single combats between champions dominate the narrative, while the masses of soldiers are described mainly in poetic summaries of slaughter.

Bhishma — Fall on Day 10 and Death After: Bhishma, Kaurava commander for days 1–10, fell on day 10 to Arjuna's arrows shot from behind Shikhandi.

Bhishma refused to fight Shikhandi because Shikhandi had been born female; Shikhandi was the reborn Amba, whom Bhishma had abducted for his half-brother and whose life he ruined, and who sought his death through penance.
Shikhandi, born a daughter to Drupada and raised as a son, became male through an exchange of sex with the yaksha Sthunakarna (Udyoga Parva, Ambopakhyana).
Bhishma himself told the Pandavas, on the night of day 9, how he could be brought down.
Bhishma had the boon of choosing the time of his death (granted by his father Shantanu for his vow of celibacy), so he lay on the bed of arrows until the winter solstice.

Bhishma lay on the bed of arrows for 58 nights; in the last part of that time, after the war and Yudhishthira's coronation, he instructed Yudhishthira on dharma, kingship and liberation (Shanti and Anushasana Parvas).
Bhishma's time from fall to death: Nights on the bed of arrows 58.
Popular tradition observes Bhishma Ashtami (in the month of Magha) as the day of Bhishma's death; this calendar placement is traditional.
Abhimanyu — Day 13: Abhimanyu, son of Arjuna and Subhadra and husband of Uttara, was killed on day 13 inside Drona's Chakravyuha.
Abhimanyu killed many Kaurava warriors in the Chakravyuha, including Duryodhana's son Lakshmana and Brihadbala of Kosala.
Abhimanyu was attacked by several great warriors at once (commonly listed as Drona, Kripa, Karna, Ashwatthama, Brihadbala and Kritavarma); Karna cut his bow from behind on Drona's advice.
Disarmed and without a chariot, Abhimanyu fought on with a sword, a chariot wheel and finally a mace, and was killed by the son of Duhshasana with a mace blow to the head.
Popular retellings often speak of 'seven maharathis' surrounding Abhimanyu, with lists that vary; the Sanskrit account names the six above as the main attackers.
The Adi Parva says Abhimanyu was an incarnation of Varchas, son of the Moon god Soma, who allowed his son to stay on earth for only sixteen years.
Abhimanyu's unborn son Parikshit, carried by Uttara, became the sole heir of the Kuru line after the war.
Abhimanyu's death led to Arjuna's vow to kill Jayadratha and is widely remembered as the war's most poignant breach of fair fighting.
Jayadratha — Day 14: Jayadratha, king of Sindhu-Sauvira and husband of Duryodhana's sister Duhshala, was killed by Arjuna just before sunset on day 14.
Jayadratha had tried to abduct Draupadi during the forest exile; the Pandavas captured him, shaved his head into tufts and released him, after which he performed penance and won a boon from Shiva.
Jayadratha's boon let him hold back all the Pandavas except Arjuna for one day, which he used to seal the Chakravyuha behind Abhimanyu on day 13.
Arjuna vowed to kill Jayadratha before the next sunset or enter fire; Drona hid Jayadratha deep within a layered array.
Many versions say Krishna created a darkness resembling sunset so that Jayadratha emerged, after which the sun reappeared and Arjuna struck — details differ between recensions and popular tellings.

Jayadratha's father Vriddhakshatra had decreed that whoever caused his son's head to fall to the ground would have his own head shatter; Arjuna's arrows carried the severed head into the lap of the meditating father, who let it fall and died (details vary between versions).
Ghatotkacha — Night of Day 14: Ghatotkacha, son of Bhima and the rakshasi Hidimbi, was killed during the night battle after day 14 by Karna's Vasavi Shakti.
Ghatotkacha's rakshasa powers grew at night, and his attack threw the Kaurava army into such panic that Duryodhana begged Karna to use the Shakti.
Before his death Ghatotkacha killed the rakshasa warriors Alambusha and Alayudha, who fought for the Kauravas.
As he died, Ghatotkacha is said to have swelled to an enormous size and fallen on the Kaurava troops, crushing many of them.
Krishna rejoiced at Ghatotkacha's death because the one-time Shakti could no longer be used against Arjuna, and explained that he had long worked to protect Arjuna from it.
Ghatotkacha's sacrifice is often read as decisive for the outcome of the Karna–Arjuna duel three days later.
Drona — Day 15: Drona, Kaurava commander for days 11–15 and teacher of both Pandavas and Kauravas, was killed by Dhrishtadyumna on day 15.
Dhrishtadyumna had been born from Drupada's sacrificial fire for the express purpose of killing Drona, who nonetheless had taught him weapons.
Drona was undone by the elephant ruse: Bhima killed an elephant named Ashwatthama and Yudhishthira confirmed that Ashwatthama was dead, adding the word for elephant indistinctly.
Yudhishthira's chariot, which had always floated four fingers' breadth above the ground because of his truthfulness, touched the earth after his half-truth.

Drona laid down his weapons and entered yogic meditation; the epic says his spirit had already departed for heaven when Dhrishtadyumna beheaded him, a departure only a few (including Arjuna, Krishna, Kripa, Yudhishthira and Sanjaya) could see.
The epic describes Drona at his death as dark-complexioned, white-haired and about eighty-five years old (as commonly rendered).

Arjuna and Satyaki condemned Dhrishtadyumna for killing his unarmed teacher; Dhrishtadyumna defended the act as lawful against a brahmin who had taken up arms and used celestial weapons on ordinary soldiers.
Drona's death provoked Ashwatthama's Narayanastra and, ultimately, his night massacre in which Dhrishtadyumna was killed.
Karna — Day 17: Karna, Kaurava commander for days 16–17 and Kunti's unacknowledged eldest son, was killed by Arjuna on day 17.

Karna had given away his natural armour and earrings (kavacha-kundala) to Indra, disguised as a brahmin, receiving in return the one-time Vasavi Shakti (Vana Parva); popular retellings embellish the details of the armour and the gift.
Karna's weapons teacher Parashurama cursed him to forget the Brahmastra at the moment of greatest need after discovering that Karna was not a brahmin as he had claimed (narrated in the Shanti Parva).
A brahmin whose sacrificial cow Karna had accidentally killed cursed him that his chariot wheel would sink into the earth in his decisive battle (Shanti Parva).
Popular and regional retellings add further causes, such as a curse from the Earth goddess (Bhumi devi); these are not part of the core Sanskrit account.
In the duel, Karna's chariot wheel sank and he could not recall the Brahmastra; he asked Arjuna to wait under the rules of fair fighting while he freed the wheel.

Krishna answered by listing Karna's own breaches of dharma — Draupadi's humiliation, the rigged dice game and the killing of Abhimanyu — and urged Arjuna to strike; Arjuna killed Karna with the Anjalika arrow.
Kunti revealed Karna's identity to the Pandavas only after the war, and Yudhishthira performed his funeral rites and mourned him as their eldest brother.
Shalya — Day 18: Shalya, king of Madra and maternal uncle of Nakula and Sahadeva, was Kaurava commander on day 18 and was killed by Yudhishthira around midday.
Shalya had been won to the Kaurava side by Duryodhana's hospitality and served as Karna's charioteer on day 17, undermining him as he had promised Yudhishthira.
As commander, Shalya fought fiercely; on Krishna's advice Yudhishthira took him as his own opponent.
Yudhishthira killed Shalya with a spear (shakti) and then killed a younger brother of Shalya who attacked him.
After Shalya's death the remaining Kaurava army collapsed; Shakuni and his son Uluka were killed by Sahadeva the same day.
Duryodhana — The Mace Duel on Day 18: After his army was destroyed on day 18, Duryodhana hid in the Dvaipayana lake; the Pandavas found him and Yudhishthira challenged him to fight any one of them.
Duryodhana chose the mace and fought Bhima; both were pupils of Balarama in mace fighting, and Duryodhana was judged the more skilful.
Balarama returned from pilgrimage to watch the duel, which was fought at Samantapanchaka.
Krishna told Arjuna that Bhima could not win fairly; Arjuna slapped his own thigh as a signal, and Bhima broke Duryodhana's thighs with his mace.
Bhima had vowed at the dice game to break the thigh Duryodhana had bared to Draupadi; the sage Maitreya had also cursed Duryodhana (Vana Parva) that Bhima would break his thigh.

Balarama was furious that Bhima struck below the navel, against the rules of mace fighting, and raised his plough to attack him until Krishna calmed him; Balarama left, calling Duryodhana a straight fighter and Bhima a crooked one.
Bhima kicked the fallen Duryodhana's head, and Yudhishthira rebuked him; Duryodhana accused Krishna of winning the war by repeated deceptions, and flowers rained from the sky on him.
Krishna replied that the Kaurava champions could not have been killed by fair means and that the gods too had used such means against their foes.
The popular story that Gandhari's gaze made Duryodhana's body invulnerable except where it was covered (his thighs or loins) is a later or regional addition, not found in the Critical Edition.

Duryodhana died at the end of the night after hearing from Ashwatthama of the massacre in the Pandava camp; Yudhishthira later finds him in heaven (Svargarohana Parva) as one who died a warrior's death.
