Bhima is traditionally credited with killing all of Dhritarashtra's sons who fought (the hundred Kauravas), in fulfilment of his vow, including Duhshasana, Vikarna and finally Duryodhana; Yuyutsu, who fought for the Pandavas, was the only son of Dhritarashtra to survive.
Arjuna's most important kills were Bhishma (with Shikhandi), Bhagadatta, Jayadratha, Vrishasena and Karna.
Satyaki's ten sons were killed by Bhurishravas on day 5; Satyaki later beheaded Bhurishravas on day 14, continuing a hereditary feud between their families.
Bhagadatta of Pragjyotisha, an aged king and son of the demon Naraka, fought on a great elephant named Supratika; Arjuna killed both on day 12.
Shrutayudha was killed on day 14 by his own divine mace from Varuna, which rebounded on him when he hurled it at the unarmed Krishna.
The Sleeping Camp — Victims of the Night: In the Sauptika Parva, Ashwatthama, helped by Kripa and Kritavarma, attacked the sleeping Pandava camp on the night after day 18.
Dhrishtadyumna, Drona's killer, was killed first, trampled and beaten to death without a weapon despite begging for a warrior's death by weapon.
The five sons of Draupadi (the Upapandavas) — Prativindhya, Sutasoma, Shrutakarma, Shatanika and Shrutasena — were killed in their sleep.
Shikhandi, Uttamaujas and Yudhamanyu, and large numbers of Panchala and Matsya warriors, were also killed in the night massacre.
Night massacre named victims: Dhrishtadyumna 1 | Upapandavas 5 | Shikhandi 1 | Uttamaujas 1 | Yudhamanyu 1.
The Pandavas, Krishna and Satyaki survived because Krishna had taken them away from the camp that night; Dhrishtadyumna's charioteer escaped and brought the news.

After the massacre Ashwatthama clashed with Arjuna using the Brahmashiras weapon; he was defeated, surrendered the gem on his forehead, and was cursed by Krishna to wander the earth in suffering (for three thousand years, in the text).
Survivors of the War: Traditionally only ten warriors survived the war: seven on the Pandava side and three on the Kaurava side.
Survivors by side (traditional count): Pandava side 7 | Kaurava side 3 | Total 10.
The seven Pandava-side survivors were Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, Sahadeva, Krishna and Satyaki.
The three Kaurava-side survivors were Ashwatthama, Kripa and Kritavarma.
Counting variants: Yuyutsu, Dhritarashtra's son who fought for the Pandavas, also survived, and some counts add him; Sanjaya, a non-combatant captured on day 18 and released, also survived.
Karna's son Vrishaketu appears as a survivor in some later tellings, notably the Jaimini Ashvamedha tradition, but is not part of the traditional count.

Of the survivors, Kritavarma and Satyaki later died in the Yadava fratricide (Mausala Parva), and Kripa became teacher to the young king Parikshit; later tradition counts Ashwatthama and Kripa among the chiranjivis (long-lived immortals).
Death Toll Figures in the Epic: In the Stri Parva, Yudhishthira tells Dhritarashtra how many fell; in K. M. Ganguli's translation the slain number one billion, six hundred and sixty million and twenty thousand, with a further 24,165 described as having fled or being unaccounted for (renderings differ).
Stri Parva death toll (Ganguli's rendering): Slain 1660020000 | Fled or unaccounted 24165.

The Stri Parva toll exceeds the total of 18 akshauhinis (3,936,600 fighting units) by orders of magnitude, so scholars treat it as hyperbole rather than a count consistent with the akshauhini figures.
Of the 18 akshauhinis assembled at Kurukshetra, the epic presents both armies as annihilated except for the handful of named survivors.
Yudhishthira also tells Dhritarashtra that the warriors who fell bravely attained the worlds of the righteous, according to how they died.
Curses, Boons and Fated Deaths: Bhishma: the boon of choosing his death (from Shantanu) and Amba's vow of revenge, fulfilled through her rebirth as Shikhandi with Shiva's blessing.
Drona: Drupada performed a sacrifice to obtain a son who would kill Drona, and Dhrishtadyumna emerged from the fire for that purpose.

Karna: Parashurama's curse (forgetting the Brahmastra), the brahmin's curse (the sinking chariot wheel), and the loss of his armour and earrings to Indra; Bhishma also cited his loss of armour when rating him only half a warrior.
Jayadratha: Shiva's boon to block the Pandavas for one day, and his father Vriddhakshatra's protective decree that rebounded on the father himself.
Duryodhana: Bhima's vow at the dice game and the sage Maitreya's curse both foretold the breaking of his thigh.
Abhimanyu: the Adi Parva's account that he was the Moon god's son Varchas, allowed only sixteen years on earth, frames his early death as fated.
Ghatotkacha: Indra's one-time Shakti, obtained by Karna for Arjuna, was fated to be spent on him.
Ashwatthama: after the war Krishna cursed him to wander the earth with festering wounds, which later tradition develops into the idea that he is still alive.
The Fairness Debates: The epic does not hide the questionable means by which the Pandavas killed the Kaurava commanders; it lets the victims and onlookers voice the accusations.
Bhishma: brought down by using Shikhandi, whom he would not fight, though Bhishma himself revealed the method.
Drona: tricked with a half-truth from Yudhishthira and beheaded while meditating unarmed; even Arjuna condemned the act.
Karna: killed while trying to free his sunken chariot wheel; Krishna justified it by Karna's own past breaches of dharma.
Duryodhana: struck below the navel in a mace duel; Balarama condemned the blow, while Krishna cited Bhima's vow and argued the Kauravas could not be defeated fairly.
The Kaurava side's breaches — the joint killing of Abhimanyu and Ashwatthama's massacre of sleeping men — are condemned just as strongly, so neither side emerges with clean hands.

Interpreters differ: devotional traditions see Krishna as restoring dharma by any means necessary against greater wrongs; others read the epic as a deliberate exploration of how dharma is subtle (sukshma) and how war corrupts even the righteous.
